cmo-cmo-1974-01.title: Exponents and induction
cmo-cmo-1974-01.body:
**i)** Let $q = 1 + \frac1n > 0$, so $x = q^n$ and $y = q^{n+1}$. Then $y = q\cdot x = \frac{n+1}{n}x$ and also $y = \left(q^n\right)^{(n+1)/n} = x^{(n+1)/n}$. Hence
$$y^x = \left(x^{\frac{n+1}{n}}\right)^x = x^{\frac{n+1}{n}x} = x^{y}.$$

**ii)** Let $S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n (-1)^{k+1}k^2$ and $T_n = 1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}2$. We prove $S_n = (-1)^{n+1}T_n$ by induction. For $n = 1$: $S_1 = 1 = T_1$. If it holds for $n$, then
$$S_{n+1} = (-1)^{n+1}\frac{n(n+1)}{2} + (-1)^{n+2}(n+1)^2 = (-1)^{n}(n+1)\left[(n+1) - \frac n2\right] = (-1)^{n+2}\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2} = (-1)^{n+2}T_{n+1}.$$ ∎

cmo-cmo-1974-01.title: Pairing for part ii
cmo-cmo-1974-01.body:
Group consecutive terms: $(2j-1)^2 - (2j)^2 = -(4j - 1) = -\left[(2j - 1) + 2j\right]$. So each pair contributes minus the sum of its two indices.
- $n$ even: $S_n = -\sum_{k=1}^{n} k = -T_n = (-1)^{n+1}T_n$.
- $n$ odd: $S_n = S_{n-1} + n^2 = -T_{n-1} + n^2 = -\frac{(n-1)n}{2} + n^2 = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = (-1)^{n+1}T_n$. ∎

cmo-cmo-1974-02.title: Tangent addition
cmo-cmo-1974-02.body:
Take $AB = CD = 1$, so $BC = 3$ and $BP = PQ = QC = 1$; the angle at $C$ is right. In the right triangles $DCB$, $DCP$, $DCQ$:
$$\tan\angle DBC = \frac{DC}{BC} = \frac13,\qquad \tan\angle DPC = \frac{DC}{PC} = \frac12,\qquad \tan\angle DQC = \frac{DC}{QC} = 1,$$
so $\angle DQC = 45^\circ$. Both $\angle DBC$ and $\angle DPC$ are acute, and
$$\tan(\angle DBC + \angle DPC) = \frac{\frac13 + \frac12}{1 - \frac13\cdot\frac12} = \frac{5/6}{5/6} = 1.$$
Since the sum is less than $90^\circ$ (as $\tan\angle DBC, \tan\angle DPC < 1$, each angle is $< 45^\circ$), it equals $45^\circ = \angle DQC$. ∎

cmo-cmo-1974-02.title: Similar triangles
cmo-cmo-1974-02.body:
With $AB = 1$: $QD = \sqrt{QC^2 + CD^2} = \sqrt2$, $QP = 1$, $QB = 2$, so $QD^2 = 2 = QP\cdot QB$, i.e. $\frac{QD}{QP} = \frac{QB}{QD}$. Triangles $QDP$ and $QBD$ share the angle at $Q$, so they are similar (SAS), and $\angle QPD = \angle QDB$.

Now $\angle DQC$ is an exterior angle of triangle $BDQ$, so $\angle DQC = \angle DBQ + \angle BDQ$. Here $\angle DBQ = \angle DBC$ and $\angle BDQ = \angle QDB = \angle QPD = \angle DPC$ (since $Q$ and $C$ lie on the same ray from $P$). Hence $\angle DQC = \angle DBC + \angle DPC$. ∎

cmo-cmo-1974-03.title: Bound one factor by a0
cmo-cmo-1974-03.body:
Let $S = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n$, so $f(1) = a_0 + S$. The coefficient of $x^{n+1}$ in $f(x)^2$ comes from products $a_ia_j$ with $i + j = n + 1$ and $0 \le i, j \le n$; this forces $1 \le i \le n$ and $j = n + 1 - i$, so
$$b_{n+1} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i\,a_{n+1-i}.$$
Using $0 \le a_i \le a_0$ and $a_{n+1-i} \ge 0$,
$$b_{n+1} \le \sum_{i=1}^n a_0\, a_{n+1-i} = a_0 S.$$
Finally,
$$\frac12 f(1)^2 = \frac12(a_0 + S)^2 = a_0S + \frac12\left(a_0^2 + S^2\right) \ge a_0S \ge b_{n+1}.$$ ∎

cmo-cmo-1974-04.title: Sort and weight
cmo-cmo-1974-04.body:
The sum does not depend on the order of the $x_i$, so assume $x_1 \le x_2 \le \cdots \le x_n$. Then $|x_i - x_j| = x_j - x_i$ for $i < j$, and $x_k$ appears with sign $+$ in the $k - 1$ pairs where it is the larger and with sign $-$ in the $n - k$ pairs where it is the smaller:
$$\sum_{i<j}|x_i - x_j| = \sum_{k=1}^n (2k - n - 1)\,x_k.$$
Since $0 \le x_k \le 1$, each term is at most $\max(0,\, 2k - n - 1)$, so
$$\sum_{i<j}|x_i - x_j| \le \sum_{k > \frac{n+1}{2}} (2k - n - 1).$$
- $n = 2m$: $k = m+1, \ldots, 2m$ give $1 + 3 + \cdots + (2m - 1) = m^2 = \frac{n^2}{4}$.
- $n = 2m + 1$: $k = m+2, \ldots, 2m+1$ give $2 + 4 + \cdots + 2m = m(m+1) = \frac{n^2 - 1}{4}$.

Equality holds when $x_k = 0$ for $k \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ and $x_k = 1$ for the rest.

**Answer: $S(n) = \left\lfloor \frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor$** ($\frac{n^2}{4}$ for even $n$, $\frac{n^2-1}{4}$ for odd $n$). ∎

cmo-cmo-1974-04.title: Convexity: push to the endpoints
cmo-cmo-1974-04.body: As a function of one variable $x_i$ (others fixed), the sum is a sum of functions $|x_i - c|$, hence convex, so its maximum on $[0, 1]$ is attained at $x_i = 0$ or $x_i = 1$. Replacing the variables one at a time by the better endpoint never decreases the sum, so the maximum is attained with every $x_i \in \{0, 1\}$. If $k$ of them equal $1$, the sum is the number of pairs $\{0, 1\}$, i.e. $k(n - k)$, which is maximal for $k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$: $S(n) = \lfloor n/2\rfloor \lceil n/2 \rceil = \left\lfloor\frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor$. ∎

cmo-cmo-1974-05.title: Midpoints and a homothety
cmo-cmo-1974-05.body:
Since $AB$ is a diameter, $t_a$ and $t_b$ are both perpendicular to $AB$, hence parallel. $t_x$ is not parallel to them (as $X \ne A, B$), so it meets $t_a$ at $M$ and $t_b$ at $N$.

**$M$ is the midpoint of $AY$.** $\angle AXB = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle), so $\angle AXY = 90^\circ$. The tangent lengths from $M$ are equal: $MA = MX$, so $\angle MXA = \angle MAX$. Then
$$\angle MXY = 90^\circ - \angle MXA = 90^\circ - \angle MAX = \angle MYX$$
(the last step uses the angle sum in right triangle $AXY$), so $MX = MY$. Hence $MA = MY$ and $M$ is the midpoint of $AY$. In the same way ($\angle BXZ = 90^\circ$, $NB = NX$) $N$ is the midpoint of $BZ$.

**Conclusion.** $AY$ and $BZ$ lie on the parallel lines $t_a$, $t_b$, and $t_x = MN$ joins their midpoints.
- If $\vec{AY} = \vec{BZ}$, then $ABZY$ is a parallelogram and $YZ \parallel AB$; also $\vec{AM} = \frac12\vec{AY} = \frac12\vec{BZ} = \vec{BN}$, so $MN \parallel AB$. All three lines are parallel.
- Otherwise $YZ$ is not parallel to $AB$ (if it were, $Y$ and $Z$ would be equally far from $AB$ on the same side, making $\vec{AY} = \vec{BZ}$), so they meet at a point $K$. The homothety with centre $K$ mapping $A$ to $B$ maps line $t_a$ to the parallel line through $B$, namely $t_b$, and maps $Y$ (on line $KY$) to the intersection of line $YZ$ with $t_b$, namely $Z$. It therefore maps the midpoint $M$ of $AY$ to the midpoint $N$ of $BZ$, so $K$, $M$, $N$ are collinear: $t_x$ passes through $K$. The three lines are concurrent. ∎

cmo-cmo-1974-05.title: Coordinates
cmo-cmo-1974-05.body:
Let the circle be the unit circle, $A = (-1, 0)$, $B = (1, 0)$, so $t_a: x = -1$, $t_b: x = 1$, and let $X = (\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$ with $\sin\varphi \ne 0$; put $u = \tan\frac\varphi2$. Line $AX$ has slope $\frac{\sin\varphi}{1 + \cos\varphi} = u$, so $Z = (1, 2u)$; line $BX$ has slope $\frac{\sin\varphi}{\cos\varphi - 1} = -\frac1u$, so $Y = \left(-1, \frac2u\right)$. The tangent $t_x$ is $x\cos\varphi + y\sin\varphi = 1$.

- If $\cos\varphi = 0$ ($u = \pm 1$): $Y = (-1, \pm2)$, $Z = (1, \pm 2)$, $t_x: y = \pm1$ — all parallel to $AB$.
- Otherwise $t_x$ meets $AB$ ($y = 0$) at $x = \frac1{\cos\varphi}$. Line $YZ$: $y - 2u = \left(u - \frac1u\right)(x - 1)$ meets $y = 0$ at $x = 1 - \frac{2u^2}{u^2 - 1} = \frac{1 + u^2}{1 - u^2} = \frac1{\cos\varphi}$. Same point, so the lines are concurrent. ∎

cmo-cmo-1974-06.title: Work modulo 8
cmo-cmo-1974-06.body:
Since $15 \equiv -1 \pmod 8$, an amount $N = 8a + 15b$ ($a, b \ge 0$) satisfies $b \equiv -N \pmod 8$.

**97 is unattainable.** $97 \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, so we would need $b \equiv -1 \equiv 7 \pmod 8$, i.e. $b \ge 7$; but $15\cdot 7 = 105 > 97$.

**Every $N \ge 98$ is attainable.** Choose $b \in \{0, 1, \ldots, 7\}$ with $b \equiv -N \pmod 8$. Then $N - 15b \equiv N + b \equiv 0 \pmod 8$ and $N - 15b \ge 98 - 105 = -7$; being a multiple of $8$ greater than $-8$, it is $\ge 0$. So $N = 8a + 15b$ with $a = \frac{N - 15b}{8} \ge 0$.

**Answer: $97$ cents.**

cmo-cmo-1974-06.title: Smallest amount in each residue class
cmo-cmo-1974-06.body:
The amounts $15b$ for $b = 0, 1, \ldots, 7$ are $0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 105$, with residues $0, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 \pmod 8$ — one in each class. In the class of $15b_r$, any attainable amount $8a + 15b$ has $b \equiv b_r \pmod 8$, so $b \ge b_r$ and the amount is $\ge 15b_r$; conversely every amount $15b_r + 8a$ is attainable. So the attainable amounts in each class are exactly those $\ge 15b_r$, and the largest unattainable amount overall is
$$\max_r\,(15b_r - 8) = 105 - 8 = 97.$$
(This is the classical formula $8\cdot 15 - 8 - 15 = 97$.)

**Answer: $97$ cents.**

cmo-cmo-1974-07.title: Timetable of the buses at P
cmo-cmo-1974-07.body:
The route is $12$ miles long and takes $20$ minutes, so a bus covers a mile in $\tau = \frac53$ minutes. Measure time in minutes so that Bus 1 leaves the terminus at times $0, 20, 40, \ldots$; Bus 2 leaves (and arrives) at $10, 30, 50, \ldots$ Bus 1 always reaches the terminus at a multiple of $20$, Bus 2 at $10 \bmod 20$. Everything is periodic with period $20$, and the man's journey ends at the first terminus arrival of a bus he can still catch. The worst case is to arrive at $P$ just after a useful bus has left.

**Symmetry.** A point on the circle at position $x$ along Bus 1's route is at position $12 - x$ along Bus 2's route, and Bus 2 runs Bus 1's schedule shifted by $10$ minutes; on the straight road positions $d$ and $12 - d$ are the same point for both buses. Hence $w(12 - x) = w(x)$, and it suffices to take $0 < x \le 6$.

**Point on the circle, $1 < x \le 6$.** Write $\alpha = x\tau$. Bus 1 passes $P$ at times $\equiv \alpha$ and arrives at the terminus at the next multiple of $20$ (travel $(12 - x)\tau = 20 - \alpha$). Bus 2 passes at times $\equiv 10 - \alpha \pmod{20}$ and needs only $\alpha$ more minutes, arriving at $\equiv 10$.

- *$1 < x \le 3$ ($\alpha \le 5$).* In one period: Bus 1 passes at $\alpha$ (arrives at $20$), Bus 2 at $10 - \alpha \ge \alpha$ (arrives at $10$). So for any arrival up to $10 - \alpha$ he reaches the terminus at $10$; just after $10 - \alpha$ his best is the next Bus 2 at $30 - \alpha$ (arrives $30$; Bus 1 at $20 + \alpha$ would arrive at $40$). Worst case: $w = 30 - (10 - \alpha) = 20 + \alpha = 20 + \frac53x$.
- *$3 \le x \le 6$ ($5 \le \alpha \le 10$).* Now Bus 2 passes at $10 - \alpha \le \alpha$ (arrives $10$), then Bus 1 at $\alpha$ (arrives $20$), then Bus 2 at $30 - \alpha$ (arrives $30$). Arriving just after $10 - \alpha$: best is Bus 1, journey $20 - (10 - \alpha) = 10 + \alpha$. Arriving just after $\alpha$: best is Bus 2 at $30 - \alpha$ (arrives $30$), journey $30 - \alpha$. So $w = \max(10 + \alpha, 30 - \alpha) = 30 - \alpha = 30 - \frac53x$ (as $\alpha \le 10$).

**Point on the straight road, $0 < x \le 1$** (distance $d = x$ from the terminus). Buses pass $P$ in both directions; per period: Bus 1 out at $d\tau$, Bus 2 back at $10 - d\tau$ (arrives $10$), Bus 2 out at $10 + d\tau$, Bus 1 back at $20 - d\tau$ (arrives $20$). A returning bus always arrives first, and returning buses pass every $10$ minutes, so the worst case is to just miss one: $w = 10 + d\tau = 10 + \frac53 x$. (At $x = 0$ he is already at the terminus.)

**Results.**
- $w(2) = 20 + \frac{10}{3} = \frac{70}{3} = 23\frac13$ minutes.
- $w(4) = 30 - \frac{20}{3} = \frac{70}{3} = 23\frac13$ minutes.
- Maximum: on $(1, 3]$, $w$ rises to $25$; on $[3, 6]$ it falls to $20$; on $(0,1]$ it is at most $11\frac23$. So the longest time is $w = 25$ minutes, at $x = 3$ and (by symmetry) $x = 9$.

**Graph** ($w$ in minutes):
$$w(x) = \begin{cases} 10 + \frac53x, & 0 < x \le 1 \\ 20 + \frac53 x, & 1 < x \le 3 \\ 30 - \frac53 x, & 3 \le x \le 6 \\ 10 + \frac53 x, & 6 \le x \le 9 \\ 40 - \frac53 x, & 9 \le x < 11 \\ 30 - \frac53 x, & 11 \le x < 12 \end{cases}$$
It is a zig-zag symmetric about $x = 6$: rising from $10$ to $11\frac23$ on the straight road, jumping at $Q$ to just above $21\frac23$, rising to the peak $25$ at $x = 3$, falling to $20$ at $x = 6$, rising to $25$ at $x = 9$, falling to $21\frac23$ just before $Q$ ($x = 11$), where it drops back to $11\frac23$, and then falling towards $10$ as $x \to 12$.
